absent: Full definitions of iterator, run queue extension, task extension, dispatch queue, and scheduler structures beyond fields touched by these fragments.
Concrete numeric values of dispatch queue identifiers, enqueue flags, task flags, run queue flags, operation states, and iterator batch size.
Complete enable state enumeration and allowed transitions beyond atomic exchange mechanics.
Implementation and locking contracts of run queue lock, dispatch queue lock, and deferred notification primitives.
Behaviour of control group iteration helpers, scheduler class selection, slice out of band handling, and operation callbacks.
Error handling policy for scheduler errors and warnings beyond fallback to the global queue.
Exact preconditions for entering deferred processing from balance, wakeup, and dispatch contexts.

findings.text: Locked task iteration service for transitions while a scheduler is loaded or unloaded. It advances an iterator, excludes tasks bound to the idle scheduler class and tasks already marked dead from the extension viewpoint, then locks the run queue of the first eligible task and records that queue and task in the iterator before returning it. When no eligible task remains it reports exhaustion.

Scheduling service for deferred reenqueue work against a dispatch queue. It ignores requests while bypassing, validates capability for local targets, appends per processor deferred nodes to the owning run queue lists with accumulated flags, and then triggers deferred execution either on the already locked queue through a cheap path or on a remote queue through a cross processor notification.
Balance callback entry that executes pending deferred work for a run queue. It serves as the hook invoked from scheduling balance processing to drain locally queued dispatch and reenqueue actions.

Global task iteration periodically releases its lock and yields the processor after a fixed count of steps. This bounds the duration of a single locked scan when many tasks exist and allows rescheduling between batches.

Iteration has two modes. When a control group context is present it walks descendant groups in preorder and enumerates member tasks including dead ones through control group iteration helpers. Otherwise it walks a global membership list from a movable cursor, skipping cursor markers and stopping at a global sentinel.

Extension enable state lives in a single atomic variable. One helper unconditionally exchanges it and returns the prior value, while another helper conditionally exchanges only from an expected prior value and reports success or failure.

Waiting for an operation state change spins with processor relaxation until the observed state differs from the supplied value. The read uses acquire ordering to pair with release updates performed by dispatch paths.

Deferred processing for a run queue follows a fixed order: first direct dispatch locals destined elsewhere, then deferred local reenqueue requests if any are pending, then deferred user queue reenqueue requests if any are pending, and finally rejection handling.

Direct dispatch deferral drains one entry at a time from the head rather than using a safe list walk, because handling one entry may temporarily drop the run queue lock. Each entry carries destination queue identity plus enqueue flags with slice and virtual time, is unlinked and cleared from direct dispatch state, resolved to a concrete queue, and then forwarded to local dispatch when the resolved target is local.

Dispatch queue resolution distinguishes several identifier families: the current local queue, a local queue on a named processor, the global queue, and user created queues. Invalid processor selection, missing user queues, and unreachable builtin identifiers fall back to the global queue for the task processor and raise a scheduler error for diagnosis.

Dispatch to a local queue uses a fast path when source and destination and current queue coincide, enqueueing directly with flags to apply slice and clear operation state. Otherwise it publishes the current processor as holder, releases operation state so a concurrent dequeue can proceed, switches run queue locks to the source, and then either completes locally, falls back to global when the task cannot run remotely, or migrates the task to the destination, requesting rescheduling on the destination when the moved task outranks its current occupant.

Slice and virtual time application gives an explicit nonzero slice precedence and stores it, clearing a pending out of band slice request unless the slice is a carried default refill. When no slice is supplied and none is stored, a minimal unit is stored to avoid zero. Virtual time is stored only for priority queue enqueues.

Dispatch enqueue resolves local identifiers to the concrete owner queue, sanitizes flags, and locks only non owner queues with optional nesting. Builtin queues reject virtual time ordering. Priority queue insertion maintains both tree and list order with a fast head pointer, while first in first out insertion supports head and preempt placement with special handling for protected tasks on owner queues. Each enqueue bumps a sequence used by iteration, records custody, and optionally clears operation state with release ordering after custody handling.

Head insertion on non owner queues places the newcomer at the front and reports a head change. On owner queues it scans past leading protected tasks under run queue lock stability and inserts after them, reporting whether the newcomer actually reached the front. Iterator cursor nodes encountered during the scan are skipped with a diagnostic.

Queue length accounting increments the queued count with single write semantics for lockless readers. Immediate delivery marking is persisted for local queues and counted per run queue; when the local queue already holds more than one task or the run queue is not open, a local reenqueue is scheduled. Immediate marking on non local queues is treated as a fallback case with a diagnostic.

Reenqueue scheduling separates local and user queues. Local requests target the owning run queue and its per processor deferred node; user requests target the calling processor queue and the per processor node of the addressed queue. Nodes already queued gain additional flags by accumulation, with memory ordering that pairs with the corresponding deferred processing paths.

Deferred scheduling on an already locked queue prefers existing scheduler hooks over cross processor notification. Wakeup context needs no action because a later wakeup completion will run the work, an already pending balance callback needs no duplicate, dispatch context only marks pendency for the dispatcher to install, and only when no hook applies does it queue a notification on the target processor.

Custody tracks whether a task remains under scheduler care. Leaving custody succeeds only when the custody mark is present and the task is not in the middle of an internal migration; migration is recognized by a nonnegative sticky processor value that is set before deactivation and cleared on arrival at the destination.

Diagnostic helpers format a named event counter with fixed width fields for readable dumps, and account events by incrementing a per processor statistic for the current scheduler plus emitting a trace record with the event name and count.

A small inline wrapper resolves the current root scheduler under read side protection and forwards a local reenqueue request for the given run queue. A missing root is treated as a diagnostic condition with no further action.

Run queue locking is mandatory around direct dispatch deferral draining and around deferred scheduling decisions on a locked queue, enforced by assertions. Dispatch enqueue locks only queues not owned by a run queue, using a nested level when requested, while owner queues rely on the held run queue lock. Deferred reenqueue lists are guarded by a dedicated per queue lock with interrupt state saved.

Operation state coordination uses release stores when clearing dispatching or queueing and acquire loads when waiting, so waiters observe custody and flag updates. Cross queue dispatch avoids deadlock with concurrent dequeue by publishing a holder processor identity before releasing operation state, then reacquiring the source queue lock and verifying that the holder identity still matches before moving the task.

Observed state includes an iterator with a movable list cursor plus a step counter and optional control group traversal position, current locked queue with its lock flags and locked task; a per run queue extension area with a local dispatch queue, deferred lists for direct dispatch and reenqueue, flags for wakeup and dispatch and pending callbacks, a notification object and an immediate task count; per task extension state with operation state, queue membership and ordering nodes, slice and virtual time, flags for custody and protection and immediacy, holder and sticky processor markers, and deferred dispatch parameters.

Observed dispatch queue state includes an identifier, a lock, a list of queued tasks, an optional priority tree with a cached head pointer for fast lookup, a monotonically increasing sequence with per task sequence capture, a queued count, and per processor storage for deferred reenqueue nodes. Per scheduler processor state holds event counters and deferred local reenqueue nodes.

Task operation state moves from queueing or dispatching to none when dispatch enqueue completes, with the clearing step ordered after custody updates to avoid concurrent flag modification with dequeue. Direct dispatch uses a holder handoff where the holder mark is set before clearing and reset to an invalid processor after the move, allowing dequeue to detect transfer versus completion.

Queue and scheduler lifecycle states include task liveness where a dead marker set under run queue lock excludes tasks from locked iteration, queue validity where an invalid identifier triggers fallback to global, terminal queues where global and bypass cause custody exit and a dequeue notification while other queues retain custody, and deferred run queue flags that move among wakeup, dispatch, and pending callback before notification.

Fatal and diagnostic paths include a fatal abort if global list iteration fails to reach its sentinel, warnings for mismatched local resolution, destroyed queue dispatch, builtin virtual time use, mixed first in first out and priority use of one queue, misplaced immediate marking, and missing root scheduler, plus scheduler errors for unknown queue identifiers and disallowed reenqueue targets.

Concurrency hazards addressed include long locked scans mitigated by periodic unlock with voluntary reschedule, temporary run queue release during deferred local dispatch requiring head by head draining, iterator cursor markers that must be skipped rather than treated as tasks, and lockless reads of queue length and first task that require single write updates and ordered publication.

Dispatch queue identities observed include SCX_DSQ_LOCAL for the current processor queue and SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL for the shared queue and SCX_DSQ_INVALID for a destroyed queue and SCX_DSQ_BYPASS for terminal bypass, with additional rescue and reject flavours. Addressing uses SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON with SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_CPU_MASK for a named processor and SCX_DSQ_FLAG_BUILTIN to mark builtin queues. Enqueue controls include SCX_ENQ_HEAD with SCX_ENQ_PREEMPT for front placement and SCX_ENQ_DSQ_PRIQ for ordered insertion and SCX_ENQ_APPLY_SLICE with SCX_ENQ_CLEAR_OPSS for commit and SCX_ENQ_SLICE_DFL with SCX_ENQ_NESTED with SCX_ENQ_IMMED with SCX_ENQ_GDSQ_FALLBACK for special handling.

Task iteration uses SCX_TASK_ITER_BATCH for batch size and SCX_TASK_CURSOR to mark cursor nodes and CSS_TASK_ITER_WITH_DEAD for control group enumeration. Liveness uses SCX_TASK_DEAD and operation states include SCX_OPSS_NONE with queueing and dispatching phases. Task marks include SCX_TASK_IN_CUSTODY with SCX_TASK_PROTECTED with SCX_TASK_IMMED, and run queue context uses SCX_RQ_IN_WAKEUP with SCX_RQ_IN_DISPATCH with SCX_RQ_BAL_CB_PENDING.
